summary: POC scoping focused on workload characterization and traffic modeling for Cedar Pay's conversational payments assistant. Discussed QPS/concurrency targets, token distributions, benchmark plans, and timelines for a 3-month pilot. Key success criteria: 99th percentile latency under 350ms for hosted path, functional parity with current model, and cost within target budget. Agreed next steps to exchange traffic histograms, run end-to-end benchmarks, and share pricing/SoW.
topics: workload profile: QPS, concurrency, peak vs baseline
input/output token distributions and payload shapes
benchmark plan: harness, metrics, success criteria
deployment options: hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC)
security and compliance considerations (KMS, audit logs, SOC2)
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: All right, hello everyone, Jordan from Redwood. Thanks for taking the time. Can we do quick intros?
[00:05] Amir Qureshi: Amir, Head of ML at Cedar Pay. We're looking to POC conversational payments UX, mostly fraud flags, balance lookups, and small talk.
[00:13] Lisa Nguyen: Lisa, Platform Eng, I'll own the infra pieces.
[00:17] Ben Turner: Ben, Product — focusing on success metrics.
[00:20] Rita Gomez: Rita, Security. I'll have questions around keys and audit.
[00:25] Jordan Lee: Great, and from Redwood we have Sofia and Evan, and Priya on success. Quick agenda: define success criteria, get traffic numbers (QPS/concurrency), token distributions, benchmark plan and timeline. Sound good?
[00:38] Ben Turner: Yep. We're especially sensitive to latency on the payment flow, so 99th percentile needs to be tight.
[00:44] Sofia Patel: Understood. Could you share current numbers — baseline QPS, peak, and typical concurrency?
[00:50] Amir Qureshi: Yeah, right now our staging assistant averages about 18 QPS during business hours, peaks around 115 QPS for short windows. Concurrency per model server is around 12 for the main flow, but end-to-end concurrency with downstream calls hits about 20.
[01:07] Evan Morris: When you say peaks, are those sustained or spikes?
[01:10] Amir Qureshi: Mostly spikes — campaign bursts and promo pushes. Spikes last a minute to ten minutes. The distribution is heavy-tailed — P95 is 70 QPS, P99 around 110.
[01:19] Lisa Nguyen: Also note we do a lot of small messages — avg input tokens 25–45, output tokens avg 80–140, but in some refund flows outputs go up to 400 tokens.
[01:32] Sofia Patel: Cool. So we need the token histogram — percentiles. Do you have 50/90/95/99 numbers?
[01:37] Amir Qureshi: I can export that. Off top: input tokens median 30, P90 60, P95 85, P99 140. Output median 105, P90 220, P95 300, P99 420.
[01:49] Jordan Lee: That's super helpful. For modeling we'll treat the 99-tail separately. For the POC we usually recommend sizing for sustained baseline plus headroom for 2x burst, and then run stress tests for P99 behavior.
[02:02] Ben Turner: What are typical Redwood targets for 99p latency? We currently require under 350ms for the critical path.
[02:08] Sofia Patel: For hosted inference on similar models we consistently see 99p token latency under 250–400ms depending on model size and batch settings. If you need sub-350ms end-to-end we may need Dedicated capacity or GPU profile tuning — and careful batching/caching.
[02:22] Rita Gomez: On security, we'll want KMS integration and audit logs. Also SSO for the console.
[02:28] Evan Morris: We support KMS/HSM integrations and per-request audit logging; will share SOC2 docs.
[02:33] Amir Qureshi: Nice. Back to workload: our traffic mix is 65% short Q/A where outputs <150 tokens, 25% medium flows 150–300 tokens, 10% long flows >300 tokens (refunds and dispute summaries).
[02:45] Sofia Patel: Great — we'll model that as three buckets for the benchmark harness. We'll need sample payloads so the tokenizer behavior matches.
[02:53] Jordan Lee: For the POC success criteria let's draft something: 1) functional parity — generated responses meet our quality thresholds on the evaluation set, 2) performance — P99 end-to-end <350ms on baseline traffic and under 500ms during defined bursts, 3) cost — under $0.XX per 1k effective tokens (customer to provide target), 4) security — KMS and audit logs in place. Customer agree?
[03:16] Ben Turner: Sounds right; we'll put exact cost target in the spreadsheet.
[03:20] Amir Qureshi: One question — hosted or dedicated? We prefer hosted for speed of onboarding but might need dedicated if the 99p is not reachable.
[03:28] Jordan Lee: We can pilot on hosted with a dedicated model profile; if latency or isolation needs require it we can propose Dedicated capacity — reserved GPUs. That will help hit sub-350ms consistently.
[03:39] Lisa Nguyen: For VPC/private deployment: we need to know about peering times and network egress requirements. Our security team rarely allows external endpoints in prod.
[03:46] Priya Raman: Noted. We'll document networking options and typical peering lead times.
[03:51] Sofia Patel: For workload sizing I want to propose baseline config: assuming average tokens per request (in+out) is ~140 tokens, baseline QPS 18 -> baseline tps (tokens/sec) equals 18 * 140 = 2520 tokens/sec. Peak burst 2x -> 5040 tokens/sec. We'll map that to GPU throughput numbers in the benchmark.
[04:09] Amir Qureshi: Our token accounting is slightly different — we charge by input and output separately but for capacity we need combined. Also note we have a lot of short, high-frequency health-check style calls where outputs are tiny but QPS is high.
[04:22] Sofia Patel: We'll include a separate small-payload bucket: input+output ~40 tokens but QPS high — that affects batching behavior.
[04:29] Ben Turner: How do you model concurrency? We have async downstream lookups that add 50–150ms sometimes.
[04:36] Evan Morris: We model application concurrency as the number of in-flight requests. If downstream adds latency that increases E2E concurrency needs and we may need more replicas or lower batch sizes to meet P99.
[04:46] Sofia Patel: Right — we'll run an end-to-end (frontend -> Redwood -> downstream) benchmark to capture that tail. For the POC we recommend capturing these metrics: 50/90/95/99 latency, CPU/GPU utilization, token throughput, batching statistics, cache hits for prefix/KV cache, and cost per 1k tokens.
[05:02] Amir Qureshi: Can you share the benchmark harness and the script to replay traffic with the same timing?
[05:07] Sofia Patel: Yes — we'll share a JMeter-based harness and a small python replay that reads timestamped CSV traffic. We'll also include instructions to swap in sample payloads and tokenizers.
[05:15] Jordan Lee: On the model side, which model family are you evaluating?
[05:18] Amir Qureshi: We're testing 13B-flavor open models today that we host internally; for Redwood we want to try 34B and 13B candidates — cost vs latency tradeoff is important.
[05:27] Sofia Patel: Good. 13B typically gives lower latency but might struggle on complex refund summarizations. 34B will push latency up but may reduce hallucinations. For capacity modeling we'll run both under identical traffic and look at quality delta on your eval set.
[05:39] Ben Turner: What's the usual pilot timeline?
[05:42] Jordan Lee: Typical is 4–8 weeks: week 0–1 exchange data and set success criteria, week 2 benchmark and initial tuning, week 3 iterate on models/config and run scaled tests, week 4 review and decide on expansion or Dedicated sizing. For enterprise customers who need Private deploy, add 2–4 weeks for networking and security reviews.
[06:00] Amir Qureshi: 4–8 weeks is reasonable. We want to ensure we can run an A/B against current internal model during the pilot.
[06:07] Sofia Patel: We'll help set up side-by-side evaluation and the metrics to compare (latency, quality on labeled prompts, F1 on extraction tasks).
[06:15] Rita Gomez: On keys: our requirement is that customer-managed KMS be used for production tokens. For pilot we can accept managed KMS if audit trails are turned on.
[06:25] Jordan Lee: That's doable. We'll share the KMS integration doc and note which pieces are customer-managed vs Redwood-managed for pilot vs prod.
[06:31] Ben Turner: Can we capture cost modeling? If we run 18 QPS baseline, average tokens 140, that's about X million tokens per day — can you estimate monthly cost?
[06:41] Sofia Patel: We'll produce a cost model. Quick calc: 18 QPS * 3600 * 24 = 1,555,200 requests/day. At 140 tokens/request that's ~217.7M tokens/day. Multiply by your per-1k token target to get monthly. We'll refine with per-model cost and batching improvements which typically reduce billed units.
[07:02] Amir Qureshi: We also do scheduled overnight batch runs for summarization — that's high throughput but latency-insensitive. Could that run on cheaper quantized variants?
[07:11] Evan Morris: Yes, offline/batch workloads are good candidates for quantized models or cheaper hardware; Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization profile and batching for those.
[07:19] Lisa Nguyen: For benchmarking network, what's the expected egress during tests? We'll need to schedule peering windows.
[07:25] Jordan Lee: We'll provide expected IP ranges and bandwidth estimates based on your peak QPS and token sizes. Also recommend running benchmark from within your VPC to capture real network path.
[07:36] Ben Turner: Ok. About SLA — if we go Dedicated, what's typical uptime guarantee?
[07:40] Priya Raman: Dedicated customers get SLA options; we'll share the SLA tiers in the pricing doc. For the POC you'll get support but not the final SLA — that's tied to contractual terms.
[07:51] Amir Qureshi: Are there any gotchas with KV cache/prefix cache? Our flows reuse previous context a lot.
[07:58] Sofia Patel: Prefix/KV caching helps a lot for repeated contexts. We'll instrument cache hit rates — if you have long-lived sessions we can reduce compute significantly. Note that cache warmup affects early tail; we'll simulate session patterns in the harness.
[08:15] Ben Turner: For bench runs, can we test both hosted and dedicated to compare latency/cost?
[08:20] Jordan Lee: Yes — we usually run hosted first then Dedicated to compare. We'll need a short window to provision Dedicated GPUs if you go that route.
[08:29] Amir Qureshi: Regarding success criteria on quality: we'll share a set of 300 evaluation prompts with labels and thresholds. We want at least parity within 5% of current model on our main metrics.
[08:40] Sofia Patel: Perfect — we'll run those evals and put them in the benchmark report.
[08:45] Lisa Nguyen: Any network security checklist we should expect?
[08:48] Priya Raman: We'll send a checklist: VPC peering, IP allowlist, mutual TLS for private endpoints, KMS requirements, audit log retention.
[08:58] Rita Gomez: Also SOC2 documents and data residency statements for EU.
[09:02] Jordan Lee: We'll attach the SOC2 and a data residency note.
[09:07] Ben Turner: Timeline recap?
[09:09] Jordan Lee: Week 0–1: exchange histograms, sample payloads, and success criteria. Week 2: Redwood shares harness and runs initial hosted benchmarks. Week 3: scale tests and tuning. Week 4: review and decision. We agreed on 4 weeks to start.
[09:22] Amir Qureshi: Ok. We'll get you the token histograms and the eval set by Friday (2027-10-07).
[09:28] Jordan Lee: Great. We'll share pricing and SoW by Wednesday (2027-10-06) and Sofia will send the harness by Friday (2027-10-08).
[09:35] Sofia Patel: One more note on modeling: when we simulate bursts we'll run varied inter-arrival distributions (poisson, pareto) to capture heavy tails. Also we'll simulate downstream latency by injecting synthetic delays to capture concurrency impact.
[09:48] Amir Qureshi: Good, that will surface issues.
[09:51] Ben Turner: Anything else?
[09:53] Rita Gomez: Please include contact for security review.
[09:55] Jordan Lee: I'll include Priya and Evan as points for security and infra.
[09:59] Ben Turner: Great, thanks everyone.
[10:00] Jordan Lee: Thanks — we'll follow up with the artifacts. Links: shared doc - https://redwood.app/s/cedarpay-poc-scope; benchmark harness repo - https://git.redwood.ai/cedarpay-poc/harness. End call.
